title: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL
overview: SQL command families separate schema definitions, row operations, privileges, and transaction management. This classification helps explain the effect and permission requirements of a statement.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DDL includes CREATE, ALTER, and DROP. DML commonly includes INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE; SELECT is sometimes classified separately as DQL. DCL includes GRANT and REVOKE. TCL includes COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT.

sections.title: Practical considerations
sections.body: These are teaching categories rather than universal execution guarantees. In PostgreSQL most DDL can be rolled back, but CREATE DATABASE cannot run inside a transaction block.

interview.question: Why is DDL versus DML insufficient to predict rollback behavior?
interview.answer: The classification describes intent, not the engine’s transaction semantics. For example PostgreSQL can roll back CREATE TABLE, while some databases implicitly commit DDL. Check the specific statement and engine.

title: SELECT
overview: SELECT constructs a result set from source rows. Projection chooses columns or expressions; filtering, grouping, and ordering shape the result.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A conceptual query order is FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, then LIMIT. The optimizer may execute a different physical plan while preserving semantics.

sections.title: Practical considerations
sections.body: SELECT * couples consumers to schema changes and may fetch unnecessary data. A query without ORDER BY has no guaranteed row order, even if repeated executions appear stable.

example:
SELECT id, price * quantity AS total
FROM order_items
WHERE quantity > 0
ORDER BY total DESC;

interview.answer: Logical processing defines the meaning of clauses. An optimizer may reorder inner joins, push filters, and use indexes so long as the returned result obeys that meaning. Outer joins and volatile expressions constrain legal transformations.

title: WHERE
overview: WHERE retains rows whose predicate evaluates to TRUE before grouping. FALSE and UNKNOWN rows are excluded.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Combine predicates with AND, OR, and NOT. SQL uses three-valued logic because comparisons involving NULL usually evaluate to UNKNOWN; use IS NULL rather than = NULL.

sections.title: Practical considerations
sections.body: AND has higher precedence than OR. Explicit parentheses prevent accidental widening of a filter, especially in updates and authorization predicates.

example:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE active = true AND (department = 'Engineering' OR department = 'Data');

interview.question: Why can NOT IN unexpectedly return no rows when its subquery contains NULL?
interview.answer: NOT IN behaves like a conjunction of inequality comparisons. A NULL makes at least one comparison UNKNOWN, so candidate rows may not satisfy TRUE. Prefer NOT EXISTS with an explicit correlation when nullable values are possible.

title: ORDER BY
overview: ORDER BY gives a result set an explicit sort order. It is required when callers depend on which row appears first.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Specify ASC or DESC for each expression independently. Add a unique tie-breaker when a stable order is needed. PostgreSQL supports NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST.

sections.title: Practical considerations
sections.body: Sorting can consume memory and spill to disk. A matching B-tree index may satisfy ordering, but only if its key directions and query conditions are compatible.

example:
SELECT id, salary FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC;

interview.question: How can a database avoid an explicit sort for ORDER BY?
interview.answer: It may scan a compatible ordered index. For ORDER BY salary DESC, id ASC, an index with matching direction can help; selective filters, fetch cost, and LIMIT influence whether the optimizer chooses it.

title: DISTINCT
overview: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the projected result. Uniqueness applies to the entire selected tuple, not just its first column.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SELECT DISTINCT city, country returns unique city-country pairs. The engine can use hashing or sorting. NULL values are considered equal for duplicate elimination.

sections.title: Practical considerations
sections.body: DISTINCT can hide an incorrect join that multiplies rows. Fix the relationship or use EXISTS when asking whether a related record exists. PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON is a dialect-specific way to choose one row per key.

interview.question: When is EXISTS preferable to joining and adding DISTINCT?
interview.answer: When the question is whether at least one child exists. EXISTS expresses that directly and avoids generating a multiplied intermediate result. DISTINCT after a join may be expensive and can obscure a modeling error.

title: LIMIT
overview: LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned. It is useful for top-N queries and small pages but needs deterministic ordering to mean anything repeatable.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ORDER BY establishes the sequence before LIMIT takes a prefix. OFFSET skips a prefix, so larger offsets often require more work. SQL-standard FETCH FIRST is another supported syntax.

sections.title: Practical considerations
sections.body: Offset pagination can duplicate or skip results under concurrent inserts and deletions. Keyset pagination uses the last seen ordered key to find the next page more efficiently.

example:
SELECT id, created_at FROM events
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z', 500)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

interview.answer: Order by created_at and a unique id. Carry both values in the cursor and use a lexicographic comparison matching the order. Index both columns. Define behavior for rows whose ordering values change during traversal.

title: Aggregate Functions

title: INNER JOIN

sections.title: Practical considerations
sections.body: Joining two one-to-many relationships can multiply rows and inflate aggregates. Aggregate each child first or carefully choose the intended grain.

title: CROSS JOIN
overview: CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product: every row from one input paired with every row from the other. It deliberately has no match predicate.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: If inputs have m and n rows, the result has m × n rows. It is useful for generating combinations such as every date crossed with every store.

sections.title: Practical considerations
sections.body: A missing join predicate can accidentally create a huge product. Estimate cardinality before executing and filter or aggregate at the right stage.
